paras: The threatened lynching of Herman Schmidt took place in Chico, California, on the night of June 24, 1882, when a crowd gathered after Schmidt, a saloon keeper, was accused of shooting his wife dead. Officers misled the crowd and Schmidt was not harmed; he was tried, convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to hang within two weeks. The papers gave more attention to the speed of the court proceedings than to the crowd, and none of them stated Schmidt's race.

According to a Chico dispatch of June 24, at about nine o'clock that evening Schmidt shot his wife dead in his saloon and tried to escape. He was captured and taken to jail, where it was found that he had taken poison, and medical aid was called. The fuller version of the wire said the killing grew out of family and financial troubles and that a divorce suit was pending.

Meanwhile a crowd assembled, and the dispatch predicted that if the poison was counteracted the prisoner would 'probably be lynched before morning.' No lynching followed. A week later the Sacramento Record-Union, citing the People's Cause, wrote that 'the citizens of Red Bluff' would have lynched Schmidt that Saturday had the officers not 'misled the crowd that was ready to do the job.' How the officers misled the crowd is not described in the coverage, nor is the size of the crowd.

Schmidt's preliminary examination was held at Oroville on June 28 before Justice Leonard, where he appeared without counsel, offered no defense and was held to answer without bail on a charge of murder. An information was filed in the Superior Court the next day, and Schmidt was arraigned, assigned counsel and pleaded not guilty. On Saturday, July 1, he was tried between ten in the morning and half past twelve and found guilty of murder in the first degree, though his counsel had noted a technicality that might win a new trial.

On July 6 a Superior Court judge, named as Hundley in one copy of the dispatch and Hudley in another, sentenced Schmidt to be hanged, and he 'displayed but little feeling or emotion.' No report of a new trial or of an execution was found in the coverage.

The first reports were short wire items printed under headings such as 'A California Tragedy' in Idaho and 'A Wife Murderer' in Arizona, which treated a hanging by the crowd as a likely outcome without comment. The Sacramento Record-Union printed the People's Cause item about the crowd without comment of its own.

After the conviction the Record-Union called the case 'quick work' that gave 'the people of Butte great satisfaction.' The Oroville sentencing dispatch, carried in Sacramento and in Nevada and Montana papers, said the promptness was 'in remarkable contrast to the usual procedure of our Courts'; the Montana paper headed it 'A Speedy Death Sentence.'

The Chico wire and every court report place the killing and the jail in Chico, while the People's Cause item spoke of 'citizens of Red Bluff,' which may refer to where the would-be lynchers came from or may be an error. The Phoenix Herald's copy of the wire named the man 'Herr Snyder,' but all other reports call him Schmidt, and the Record-Union gave his full name as Herman Schmidt.

framing.detail: Headlines 'A California Tragedy' and 'A Wife Murderer' presented the threatened hanging as a likely outcome without comment.
The Record-Union passed on the People's Cause item about the crowd 'ready to do the job' without comment, then praised the quick conviction as giving 'the people of Butte great satisfaction'.
The Oroville sentencing dispatch, headed 'A Speedy Death Sentence' in Montana, contrasted the promptness with the usual delays of the courts.
